title: Beer-Lambert Law
explanation: Relates the absorbance (A) of a solution at a given wavelength to the concentration of the absorbing species (c), the path length light travels through the sample (l, commonly 1 cm for a standard cuvette), and the molar absorptivity (ε), a wavelength-specific constant for that substance. Because absorbance depends linearly on concentration only within a limited range, this relationship (and any standard curve built on it) is only valid where the instrument and sample stay within their linear range — a very concentrated sample should be diluted rather than trusted at face value.

variables.meaning: Molar absorptivity (extinction coefficient), specific to the substance and wavelength, units L·mol⁻¹·cm⁻¹
Path length light travels through the sample, in cm
Concentration of the absorbing species, in mol/L

workedExample.scenario: A solution with molar absorptivity 5,000 L·mol⁻¹·cm⁻¹ at the measurement wavelength, read in a 1 cm cuvette, gives an absorbance of 0.5.

commonMistakes: Applying the Beer-Lambert relationship outside the instrument's/sample's linear absorbance range, where the relationship between absorbance and concentration is no longer linear.
Using a molar absorptivity value for the wrong wavelength or the wrong substance/solvent combination.

Forgetting that bacterial culture turbidity (OD) readings are a light-scattering measurement, not a true molar-absorptivity-based concentration measurement — OD-to-cell-count relationships require their own empirically derived standard curve for the specific organism and instrument, not a generic Beer-Lambert calculation.
